start: If I am not for myself, who will be for me?
context: A saying of Hillel the Elder, from the Ethics of the Fathers, a Mishnaic collection of rabbinic wisdom. In three short questions it holds self-respect, responsibility to others and urgency together.
prompt: Which of the three questions do you most need to hear today?

parts: Who is wise? He who learns from all men
Who is mighty? He who controls
Who is rich? He who rejoices
Who is honored? He who honors
context: A teaching of Ben Zoma. Each question takes a quality people chase from the outside and relocates it inside a person's own conduct.
prompt: By which of these four measures do you feel richest today?

start: It is not thy duty to complete the work
context: A saying of Rabbi Tarfon. The work of repairing the world is too large for one person, but that is no excuse for not doing your part.
prompt: What unfinished work is still worth your small contribution today?

context: From the Book of Proverbs, a collection of practical wisdom in the Hebrew Bible traditionally attributed to King Solomon.
prompt: Where could a gentler word change the course of a conversation?

context: From Kohelet (Ecclesiastes), the Hebrew Bible's most philosophical book. It continues: a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to weep and a time to laugh.
prompt: What season of life are you in right now?

context: A saying of Shammai, Hillel's famously strict counterpart. Even he counsels warmth: greet everyone with a kind face.
prompt: Who could you greet more warmly today?

start: I have found nothing better for man than silence
context: A saying of Shimon, son of Rabban Gamaliel. Study matters, but what we do matters more, and too many words lead us astray.
prompt: Where could you replace talking with doing?

start: judge not thy neighbor until thou art come into his place
context: One of Hillel's best-known teachings. We cannot fairly judge a person whose circumstances we have never stood in.
prompt: Whose place have you never stood in, though you judge them?

start: In a place where there are no men
context: Another saying of Hillel. When no one else steps up, that is precisely the moment to act with integrity.
prompt: Where is no one stepping up, and could it be you?

context: A saying of Ben Azzai. Every person will have their moment, and every thing its use.
prompt: Whom have you underestimated?

start: Look not at the flask, but at what it contains
end: not even new wine in it
context: A saying of Rabbi Meir. Appearances, including age and youth, tell us little about what is inside.
prompt: Whose 'flask' have you judged without tasting the wine?

parts: He whose wisdom exceeds his works, to what is he like?
But he whose works exceed his wisdom, to what is he like?
context: A saying of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. Knowledge without deeds is a tree with a large crown and shallow roots.
prompt: Are your roots as deep as your branches are wide?

context: The inner life is described as the source from which everything else flows, and so the thing most worth guarding.
prompt: What have you been letting into your heart lately?

context: The ant has no overseer, the passage continues, yet it gathers its food in summer. Diligence needs no supervisor.
prompt: What would you do today if no one were checking?

context: Anxiety weighs a person down, and a kind word can lift them. A small thing with a large effect.
prompt: Who around you might need a good word today?

context: We become like the company we keep.
prompt: Whose company is shaping you, and in what direction?

context: An observation about body and spirit: a calm heart sustains life, while envy eats away at a person from within.
prompt: Is there any envy quietly eating at you?

context: A 'stalled ox' was a fattened animal, a feast. A simple meal among people who love each other is worth more.
prompt: Where is love more present in your life than luxury?

context: One of the most quoted lines of the Hebrew Bible. Arrogance blinds us to the edge we are walking toward.
prompt: Where might pride be blinding you?

context: Self-mastery is ranked above military conquest. Ruling one's own spirit is the harder victory.
prompt: What part of your spirit needs ruling today?

context: True friendship is constant, and family shows its worth in hard times.
prompt: Who has been there for you in adversity, and do they know it?

context: A wry observation: silence can make anyone look wise. It also gives us time to become a little wiser.
prompt: Where would silence serve you better than speech?

context: Answering before listening fully is both foolish and embarrassing.
prompt: Who deserves to be heard all the way through before you answer?

context: Patience is called discretion, and overlooking an offence is called glory.
prompt: What offence could you gracefully pass over?

context: A person's real purposes lie deep, like water in a well. It takes understanding, and good questions, to draw them up.
prompt: What deep intention in you have you not yet drawn out?

context: The righteous are not those who never fall, but those who keep getting up.
prompt: What fall do you need to rise from again?

context: The right word at the right moment is compared to golden fruit in a silver setting: beautiful because it fits.
prompt: What well-timed word could you offer someone today?

context: Two verses placed side by side that seem to contradict each other. Wisdom lies in knowing which situation you are in.
prompt: When is it wiser to answer, and when to stay silent?

context: Tomorrow is not ours to promise. Humility about the future frees us to attend to today.
prompt: What are you counting on tomorrow that you could act on today?

context: Praise means more when it comes from others. Self-praise tends to empty itself.
prompt: Could you let your work speak for itself today?

context: Good friends sharpen each other, sometimes through friction.
prompt: Who sharpens you, and whom do you sharpen?

context: Kohelet observes that human life moves in cycles. What feels unprecedented has usually been lived before.
prompt: What struggle of yours have countless others already lived through?

context: One hand full of quiet is better than two hands full of toil. Kohelet questions the endless pursuit of more.
prompt: What would a handful of quietness look like today?

context: A reflection on companionship: two people can lift each other in ways no one can alone.
prompt: Who lifts you up, and whom could you lift?

context: Endings reveal what beginnings only promise, and patience outlasts pride.
prompt: What are you rushing that would benefit from patience?

context: Nostalgia can be a way of avoiding the present. Kohelet calls the question itself unwise.
prompt: What good thing about these days are you overlooking?

context: Because life is finite, whatever we can do, we should do with our full strength now.
prompt: What deserves your full strength today?

start: the race is not to the swift
context: Kohelet notices that talent does not guarantee success. Time and chance play their part in every life.
prompt: How might you hold your successes, and failures, more humbly?

context: Often read as a call to generosity: give freely, without calculating the return, and good tends to come back.
prompt: Where could you give without expecting anything back?

context: The farmer who waits for perfect conditions never plants. Waiting for certainty can become a way of never starting.
prompt: What are you not sowing because you are watching the wind?

context: We cannot know which of our efforts will bear fruit, so we keep sowing, morning and evening.
prompt: What seeds could you keep sowing, without knowing which will grow?
